newsitem.title: Italy: Investigators probe chapel after Turin shroud saved.
newsitem.headline: Investigators probe chapel after Turin shroud saved.

text.p: Investigators searched for clues in the gutted remains of a cathedral chapel in this north Italian city on Saturday, hours after the Turin shroud, one of the Catholic world's most revered relics, was snatched from the blaze.

A devastating fire destroyed the cathedral's Guarini chapel, built in the 17th century to house the mysterious shroud, but firemen braved falling masonry and blistering heat to pluck the winding sheet to safety.

The fire, which took almost seven hours to put out, caused no injuries but inflicted major damage to the cathedral along with part of an adjacent royal palace where earlier United Nations Secretary General Kofi Annan had attended a gala dinner.

Deputy Prime Minister Walter Veltroni said after visiting the scene that initial information did not point to an arson attack but Turin's fire chief said nothing was ruled out at this stage. "Nobody is making any assumptions. We have to examine the scene today and tomorrow," Michele Ferraro told Reuters.

Cardinal Giovanni Saldarini proclaimed that the shroud had been saved by an act of God. "It's intact, it's a miracle," he said after jubilant firemen brought the silver box containing the shroud out of the blaze.

Onlookers gazed wistfully in the morning sun at the smouldering remains of the chapel, some of them expressing anger that the shroud had come so close to being completely obliterated after security precautions failed to prevent a fire.
"I am a practising Catholic and feel angry and offended that this has been allowed to happen," said Gaetano Mioli, a 52-year-old nurse who rushed to the scene after completing night duty.

Some onlookers suggested the fire might have been started on purpose and drew parallels with a blaze in 1996 which gutted Venice's Fenice opera house, now believed to have been the work of an arsonist.
The alarm was raised shortly before midnight when smoke billowing out of the chapel -- which was being restored and under scaffolding -- activated a security system in the adjoining palace.

A huge crowd gathered outside the Renaissance cathedral in the heart of this prosperous city, to watch the dramatic inferno, which lit up the night sky as flames surged through the part of the roof and started to attack the adjoining palace.
Many people wept openly as they watched the blaze take hold, but a cheer went up when news spread that the precious shroud had been salvaged.

The shroud, a piece of cloth imprinted with the image of a man's body that many Roman Catholic believers take to be the figure of Christ after his crucifixion, was stored behind bullet-proof glass in a silver box.
Fireman Mario Trematore, hosed down by water to keep the heat at bay, had to smash through the sturdy protective covering with a sledge hammer before yanking the box to safety.
"It seemed as though everything was about to collapse on top of us," Trematore said, adding: "God gave me the strength to break that glass."

Fire officials said that besides gutting the Guarini chapel, the blaze had seriously damaged part of the Cathedral's main altar and apse along with the top two floors of the royal palace's western tower, which backs on to the cathedral.
"The damage is incalculable at this point because it covers such a wide area," said Turin fire chief Ferraro.
It was not clear what art work had been destroyed in the palace-turned-museum, but officials said part of a valuable collection pictures, antique furniture and carpets had been saved.
Minister for Public Works Franco Bassanini said the total value of the damage ran to tens of millions of dollars.
Shortly before the alarm was raised, Annan had left the palace after the dinner which was also attended by former prime minister Giulio Andreotti and industrialist Giovanni Agnelli.
Annan was in Turin to inaugurate a staff college of the International Labour Organisation later on Saturday.
